Keywords: Anything, Desperately, But

outputs.L1:
I need everything else—  
anything else—  
desperately.

But I have nothing,  
shall have nothing but this:  
immediate, inescapable, and invaluable.

No one can afford THIS,  
being made here and now  
(Seattle, Washington, 17 May 1955).

MARIGOLDS.

Concise. Wooden. Orange.  
Behind them, the garage door:  
pink—paint sold under the fatuous name “Old Rose,”  
which brings a war to mind.

And the mind slides over the fence again:  
orange against pink and green.  
Uncontrollable!  
Returned of its own accord.

It can explain nothing,  
give no account.  
What good? What worth?

Dying! You have less than a second  
to live,  
to try to explain:

Say that light, in particular wavelengths  
or bundles wobbling at a given speed,  
produces the experience—

orange against pink.

Better than a sirloin steak?  
A screen by Korin?

The effect of this, taken internally.  
The effect of beauty on the mind.

There is no equivalent, least of all  
these objects,  
which ought to manifest  
a surface disorientation, pitting,  
or striae,  
admitting some plausible interpretation.

But the cost  
can’t be expressed in numbers.

Dodging between a vagrancy rap  
and the newest electrical brain-curette,  
eating what the rich are bullied into giving  
or the poor willingly share,  
depriving themselves—

more expensive than ambergris,  
although the stink isn’t as loud.

(A few wise men have said,  
“Produced the same way . . .  
vomited out by sick whales.”)

Valuable for the same qualities:  
staying power and penetration.

I’ve squandered every crying dime.
outputs.L2:
I want all that remains—  
whatever more there might be—  
with an aching urgency.  
Yet I possess nothing  
and will possess nothing except this:  
the immediate, unavoidable, priceless thing  
that nobody can afford,  
coming into existence at this very moment  
(Seattle, Washington, May 17, 1955).

MARIGOLDS—  
compact, wooden, orange.  
The garage door behind them is pink,  
coated in a paint absurdly called “Old Rose,”  
a name that summons war.

Again the mind slips across the fence:  
orange set against pink and green.  
It cannot be controlled.  
It returns by itself.

It explains nothing,  
offers no justification.  
What use is it?  
What value does it have?

Dying—  
with less than one second left  
to exist,  
to attempt an explanation:

Perhaps light, traveling in particular wavelengths  
or quivering packets at a certain speed,  
creates the perception  
of orange against pink.

Is it superior to a sirloin steak?  
To a screen painted by Korin?

What happens when this is taken inward—  
what beauty does to the mind—  
has no equal,  
especially not in these physical things.  
They should reveal  
some disturbance of their surfaces:  
pits, grooves,  
or marks that allow  
a believable explanation.

But the price  
cannot be stated numerically.  
It evades measurement,  
moving between arrest for vagrancy  
and the latest electric curette for the brain;  
surviving on what the wealthy are pressured to donate  
or what poor people freely divide,  
even at their own expense.

It costs more than ambergris,  
though its odor is less powerful.  
(A few learned men have remarked,  
“It is formed in the same fashion . . .  
thrown up by diseased whales.”)

Its worth comes from identical virtues:  
its endurance  
and its ability to penetrate.

I have wasted every last miserable cent.
outputs.L3:
The speaker is caught between an insatiable longing for everything beyond their possession and an intense awareness of the value contained in immediate experience. Although they feel a desperate need for what they do not have, the beauty before them proves impossible to dismiss. A vivid image—orange marigolds set against a pink garage door and surrounded by green—repeatedly enters the mind, seizing attention without invitation or control.

Scientific accounts of light, vision, and color may explain how such an image is perceived, but they cannot fully account for its beauty or its emotional worth. The experience exceeds the mechanisms that produce it. Its effect on the mind is more powerful than ordinary pleasures, material possessions, or even works of art that are conventionally considered valuable. The speaker therefore presents beauty as something beyond calculation: priceless, enduring, and capable of penetrating deeply into consciousness. It is so valuable that it would justify the total expenditure of the speaker’s personal resources, as though everything they possess would be a fair price for the experience of such beauty.
outputs.L4:
The speaker’s attention is seized by a simple but vivid image: orange marigolds blooming against a pink garage door. The flowers appear in surroundings marked by poverty, disorder, and the approach of death, yet their colors possess an intensity that makes the ordinary scene suddenly extraordinary. Rather than describing the sight through a clear, linear argument, the speaker moves through fragments of thought, shifting between immediate perception, private reflection, and scientific speculation. This stream-of-consciousness form reproduces the mind’s attempt to understand why a particular arrangement of color and light can exert such emotional force.

Scientific language offers possible explanations. The speaker considers how the eye receives color, how the brain processes sensation, and how matter and consciousness might combine to produce the experience called beauty. Yet these explanations remain incomplete. They may describe the physical mechanisms of sight, but they cannot fully account for the marigolds’ power. No theory can explain why these orange flowers against this pink door, at this particular moment, should seem so arresting. Beauty is therefore presented as both materially grounded and ultimately mysterious: it arises through the body and the senses, but it cannot be reduced to biology, chemistry, or logic.

The social setting makes the vision more significant. The speaker is not contemplating beauty in a museum, a garden, or some protected place of wealth and leisure. The marigolds appear amid deprivation, where practical needs are urgent and possessions are scarce. In such a context, beauty might seem useless or extravagant. It cannot remove poverty, prevent suffering, or stop death. Nevertheless, the sight has immense value precisely because it cannot be measured in economic terms. The flowers belong to no system of exchange; their beauty is freely available to anyone capable of seeing it. For a moment, the impoverished surroundings are not erased but transformed by attention.

The awareness of impending death gives the scene further urgency. Everything the speaker sees is temporary: the flowers will wither, the light will change, the painted door will fade, and the observer will die. Yet impermanence does not make the vision meaningless. On the contrary, its fragility intensifies its beauty. The moment matters because it cannot be preserved. Its value lies in the immediate encounter between the world and the perceiving mind.

Ultimately, the speaker does not solve the mystery of the marigolds. The fragmented meditation ends not with a final explanation but with an affirmation of experience. The orange flowers against the pink garage door are beautiful before they are understood, and perhaps independently of understanding. Their beauty cannot be purchased, rationalized, or made permanent, but it can still interrupt suffering and enlarge consciousness. In this way, the vision becomes evidence that aesthetic experience may transcend material deprivation, intellectual explanation, and even mortality. Though brief and inexplicable, the moment is immediate, complete, and priceless.
outputs.L5:
### Anything, Desperately, But

Mara would have done **anything** to turn back time. She replayed their final conversation each night, searching for the moment when honesty might have changed everything.

She wanted **desperately** to call him, to explain the fear behind her silence and the love hidden beneath her anger.

**But** some doors close without making a sound. By the time she found the courage to knock, no one was waiting on the other side.
